desc:
The array nums is fixed. Each query is [l, r, k] and asks for the k-th smallest value (duplicates counted, k = 1 is the minimum) among nums[l], nums[l+1], ..., nums[r] (both ends inclusive, zero-based).

Return the answer of every query in order. Sorting each slice separately is too slow when there are thousands of long queries; use a structure that answers a query in about logarithmic time.

nums = [5, 1, 4, 1, 9], queries = [[0,4,2],[1,3,3],[2,4,1]]
slice 5 1 4 1 9 -> sorted 1 1 4 5 9 -> 2nd is 1
slice 1 4 1     -> sorted 1 1 4     -> 3rd is 4
slice 4 1 9     -> sorted 1 4 9     -> 1st is 1
answer = [1, 4, 1]
constraints: 0 ≤ l ≤ r < nums.length and 1 ≤ k ≤ r - l + 1
hints: Think about what you need from a prefix: if you knew how many elements of nums[0..r] fall into any value range, how could you handle nums[l..r]?
Counts are subtractable: (count in prefix r) minus (count in prefix l-1) is the count inside the range. Compress the values to ranks and keep one counting structure per prefix.

Store all prefix versions in a persistent segment tree over ranks (each insertion creates only O(log n) new nodes). A query walks down two roots at once, comparing the left child count difference to k.
editorial: Compress the values to ranks 0..m-1. Build a persistent segment tree over the rank range: version i+1 is version i with rank(nums[i]) incremented, copying only the O(log m) nodes along one root-to-leaf path and sharing the rest. Each node stores how many elements are in its rank interval.

For a query [l, r, k], start with the roots of versions r+1 and l. The number of slice elements in the left half of the current interval is cnt(left of r+1) - cnt(left of l). If k does not exceed it, descend left in both trees; otherwise subtract it from k and descend right. At a leaf the rank is the answer.

Building takes O(n log n) time and memory, each query O(log n). Alternatives with the same flavour are a wavelet tree/matrix, a merge-sort tree with a binary search on the answer (O(log^2 n) per query), or offline processing with a Fenwick tree and a sweep over values.
solution:
def rangeKth(nums, queries):
    vals = sorted(set(nums))
    rank = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(vals)}
    m = len(vals)
    L, R, C = [0], [0], [0]          # node 0 is the shared empty tree
    roots = [0]
    for x in nums:
        pos = rank[x]
        prev = roots[-1]
        root = len(C)
        L.append(0); R.append(0); C.append(C[prev] + 1)
        cur, p = root, prev
        lo, hi = 0, m - 1
        while lo < hi:
            mid = (lo + hi) >> 1
            new = len(C)
            if pos <= mid:
                L[cur] = new
                R[cur] = R[p]
                C.append(C[L[p]] + 1)
                p = L[p]
                hi = mid
            else:
                R[cur] = new
                L[cur] = L[p]
                C.append(C[R[p]] + 1)
                p = R[p]
                lo = mid + 1
            L.append(0); R.append(0)
            cur = new
        roots.append(root)
    out = []
    for l, r, k in queries:
        a, b = roots[r + 1], roots[l]
        lo, hi = 0, m - 1
        while lo < hi:
            mid = (lo + hi) >> 1
            cnt = C[L[a]] - C[L[b]]
            if k <= cnt:
                a, b = L[a], L[b]
                hi = mid
            else:
                k -= cnt
                a, b = R[a], R[b]
                lo = mid + 1
        out.append(vals[lo])
    return out
